summary:
FloodTracer is an interactive web app that uses NISAR radar observations to explore flooding across four areas of Uruguay. Users can compare satellite passes, view detected floodwater over a map, explore estimated flood duration, and identify roads that cross flooded land. A guided story in northern Rocha explains the findings and how the analysis works.

NISAR can observe through clouds and without daylight, helping reveal surface changes when optical satellite images cannot clearly show the ground. FloodTracer compares each location with its own conditions before the storm, separates water already present, and combines repeated detections to map possible flooding.

It demonstrates one way to make radar observations more accessible. It can support decision makers to better understand past flooding and mitigate the impact of future events
details:
FloodTracer is an interactive web application that explores how NISAR radar observations can help people understand flooding. It covers four areas of Uruguay: Treinta y Tres, Laguna Merín, Río Branco / Jaguarão, and northern Rocha. A guided story introduces the Rocha case study, while an Explorer lets users choose an area, compare observation dates, switch map layers, and inspect roads that overlap detected flooding.

The analysis uses NISAR’s L band radar, which can observe through clouds and without daylight. We process terrain corrected GCOV observations and compare each location with its own radar signal before the storm. The pipeline reduces radar speckle, identifies changes consistent with water, and separates permanent water and water already present before the event. Repeated wet detections define the event footprint. Observation dates also provide estimated duration intervals, rather than exact flooding and drying times.

Quality checks are an important part of the approach. We compare detections with Sentinel-1 observations and known water from JRC Global Surface Water. ERA5 wind data helps account for conditions that make open water appear brighter to radar. In northern Rocha, we excluded one orbit after finding inconsistencies in its water classification. These comparisons help assess the method, but they do not replace independent field validation.

We developed the processing pipeline in Python using tools including NumPy, SciPy, pandas, and Rasterio. The interface uses HTML, CSS, JS, and MapLibre GL JS. Large radar datasets are processed beforehand and exported into smaller files, allowing the website to run as a static application on GitHub Pages without a backend. Street and satellite basemaps provide geographic context, and OpenStreetMap supplies the road network.

The project’s creative approach combines a guided explanation with free exploration of the same evidence. Users can move from a narrated example to comparing dates and investigating other locations themselves.

FloodTracer is a proof of concept, not an operational warning system. Its intended impact is to make radar observations easier to explore and assess, and to investigate their potential value for communities and decision-makers studying past floods. We considered cloud cover, wind, differences between orbits, observation gaps, agricultural activity, browser performance, and uncertainty. A road overlapping detected water is not necessarily impassable, and estimated drying times still need independent validation.
